item.title: New FRCS vessels to strengthen Fiji’s maritime security and fight against drug trafficking
item.description: Fijis ability to detect and disrupt drug trafficking, customs violations and the smuggling of illicit goods is expected to be strengthened with the launch of two new Customs patrol vessels, Dau Raica and Gutulei Ni Yadra costing close to $800,000. The vessels were officially launched today at the Royal Suva Yacht Club and handed over to the Fiji Revenue and Customs Service through a partnership wi
item.content:encoded:
Fijis ability to detect and disrupt drug trafficking, customs violations and the smuggling of illicit goods is expected to be strengthened with the launch of two new Customs patrol vessels, Dau Raica and Gutulei Ni Yadra costing close to $800,000.

The vessels were officially launched today at the Royal Suva Yacht Club and handed over to the Fiji Revenue and Customs Service through a partnership with Australian government.

FRCS Chief Executive Officer Udit Singh says the vessels will extend the organisations operational reach and strengthen its ability to monitor Fijis maritime waters, conduct patrols and respond to border offences.

Singh says the vessels will also support boarding and enforcement activities, strengthen surveillance and improve cooperation with other border agencies.

He says the deployment of the vessels will be determined through an inter-agency approach, taking into account high-risk areas and operational priorities, with locations such as Savusavu, Lomaiviti and the Lau Group being considered.

He says FRCS is also looking at using drones, underwater drones and improved intelligence databases to strengthen surveillance and reach remote areas without having to continuously increase staffing.

Singh says 16 FRCS officers, comprising 12 women and four men, have attained their Boat Master's Licence through a partnership involving the United Kingdom Government and the United Nations Development Programme.

Meanwhile, Australian High Commissioner Peter Roberts says the vessels are part of Australia's wider cooperation with Fiji to address transnational crime, particularly drug trafficking.

Roberts says they will also support broader maritime operations, including search and rescue activities.

Roberts says Australia's support includes the sustainment of the vessels, training and mentoring to ensure the new capability can be maintained in Fiji.

He says maritime security requires a collective effort, with the Fiji Navy, Fiji Police and FRCS working together to secure the country's borders.

FRCS Principal Customs Officer Jone Mainayau says the name Dau Raica represents a watchful observer, reflecting the responsibility of Customs officers to monitor maritime movements and identify potential threats.

He says Gutulei Ni Yadra represents a sentinel of vigilance, drawing inspiration from Fiji's seabirds, which symbolise alertness and readiness.

Pacific (Offshore) Network Superintendent Uriah Turner says the handover represents more than the provision of vessels, highlighting the importance of partnerships, information sharing and operational cooperation in addressing evolving border security threats.

Turner says the project and support teams worked alongside their Fijian counterparts over the past 12 months to make the vessels a reality.

He says the vessels' effectiveness will depend on the officers operating them and the work they carry out to protect Fiji's borders, communities and economic prosperity.

item.title: Sport can help challenge gender stereotypes and prevent violence against women - UN Women rep Davidian
item.description: Sport has an important role to play in challenging gender stereotypes and changing attitudes that contribute to violence against women. This has been highlighted by UN Women Representative Alison Davidian during the launch of the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence Campaign at Tappoo City Complex in Suva.
item.content:encoded:
Sport has an important role to play in challenging gender stereotypes and changing attitudes that contribute to violence against women.

This has been highlighted by UN Women Representative Alison Davidian during the launch of the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence Campaign at Tappoo City Complex in Suva.

Davidian says women breaking barriers in traditionally male-dominated sports such as rugby can change how society views women's abilities and what young girls believe they can achieve.

She says the documentary Breaking Ground , which features Fijiana Drua players and other women in rugby that launched today, highlights how sport can be used to challenge assumptions about women's roles and inspire the next generation.

Davidian says bringing the documentary back on the first day of the campaign is particularly meaningful, as violence against women is often sustained by attitudes and beliefs that society has come to accept as normal.

She says children grow up absorbing messages about how girls and boys should behave, their roles in society and how power should be understood.

Davidian says while there has been progress in addressing violence against women, more work is needed to change the attitudes that allow it to happen.

She refers to the latest study on violence against women in Fiji, launched by the Fiji Women's Crisis Centre last week, which found that the proportion of women who have experienced partner violence had decreased from 64 percent to 48 percent over the past 15 years.

However, she says the findings remain concerning, with almost one in two women having experienced violence from an intimate partner and almost six in 10 women experiencing emotional abuse.

Davidian says efforts to strengthen laws and policies, support survivors and assist organisations working to end violence must continue, alongside initiatives that challenge harmful gender attitudes.

She highlights the Get Into Rugby Plus programme, which uses rugby activities to teach children about power, respect and accountability.

She says the programme encourages children to reflect on how power is used, what respect means and how to handle disagreements.

Davidian also highlights changes observed in Samoa, where a survey found that 70 percent of boys initially believed sexual harassment could be the girl's fault. By the end of the programme, none of the boys surveyed held that belief.

She says the programme has also helped women coaches gain confidence in leading boys' teams, while male coaches have reported greater patience and less aggression when working with children.

However, Davidian stresses that sport must also be a safe environment for women and girls, acknowledging that discrimination and harassment can still occur.

She says Fiji Rugby adopted three policies last year covering safeguarding, workplace harassment and gender-based violence.

The 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence Campaign is organised by the Delegation of the European Union to the Pacific to commemorate the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.

item.title: Seaqaqa resident questions rush to amend Constitution while hospital faces medicine and staff shortages
item.description: A Seaqaqa resident is questioning why the government is rushing to amend the Constitution when people do not fully understand the proposed changes and Seaqaqa Hospital continues to face shortages of medicines and medical staff. He raised these concerns during the Special Committee on the Constitution Amendment Bill's second round of public consultations in the Northern Division at the Seaqaqa Sana
item.content:encoded:
A Seaqaqa resident is questioning why the government is rushing to amend the Constitution when people do not fully understand the proposed changes and Seaqaqa Hospital continues to face shortages of medicines and medical staff.

He raised these concerns during the Special Committee on the Constitution Amendment Bill's second round of public consultations in the Northern Division at the Seaqaqa Sanatan Hall.

The resident says people are under pressure to vote yes or no in the referendum.

He says the Bill should be translated in Hindi and iTaukei so people can understand the proposed changes before making a decision.

He also suggests that the process be left to the next government, giving people more time to understand what is right and what is wrong.

The resident questions why the government is pushing to amend the Constitution now, after being in office for nearly four years.

He asks where the government has been all this time and why there is now a rush to pass the Bill.

He also raises concerns about the condition of Seaqaqa Hospital, saying the government is focusing on constitutional changes while people continue to struggle to access basic healthcare services.

He says there are shortages of medicines and medical staff at the hospital.

The resident says X-ray machines are there, but there is shortage of staff and patients are told to travel to the Labasa Hospital.

He urges Committee members to visit Seaqaqa Hospital and see the conditions for themselves.

The resident says if the Prime Minister or government ministers fall sick, they can fly overseas for treatment, while poor people will die here.

He stresses that the government should also focus on improving services rather than rushing constitutional changes.
